Hybrid joints achieved an average static peak strength of approximately 61.6 kN.
Purely bonded joints had an average static peak strength of about 60.9 kN.
Purely riveted joints had a significantly lower average static peak strength of about 36.8 kN.
Fatigue life of hybrid joints reached approximately 550,000 cycles at 6000 microstrain.
Fatigue life of bonded joints was around 440,000 cycles under similar conditions.
Fatigue life of riveted joints was the lowest, about 304,000 cycles.
Initial 2 mm cracks in the bondline reduced fatigue life by up to 5%.
Curing FM300-2K adhesive at 121°C for 90 minutes under 40 psi produced optimal bond strength.
Lower curing temperatures (e.g., 66°C) resulted in semi-cured or uncured bonds with very low strength.
Failure modes varied: riveted joints failed by bearing failure, bonded joints by adhesive cracking, hybrid joints by combined mechanisms.
Rivets in hybrid joints provide a fail-safe load path after adhesive failure.
Specimens were tested using an INSTRON 1342 machine with a 100 kN load cell.
Fatigue tests used a sinusoidal load at 5 Hz with R-ratio 0.1 and block loading regime increasing strain every 100,000 cycles.
Ultrasonic A-Scanning was used to verify bondline quality.
The FM300-2K adhesive has a tensile strength of 94.2 MPa and shear strength of 54.4 MPa.
Hybrid joints showed no significant static strength improvement over bonded joints but had superior fatigue resistance.
Rivet clamping pressure and adhesive bond strength control failure mode and damage progression.
Hybrid joints can detect weak bonding early, improving repair and certification processes.
The adherends were thin carbon fiber laminates with a total thickness of 5 mm for outer adherends and 10 plies for inner adherends.
Rivet arrays tested included 6 rivets in a square pattern and 3 rivets in a staggered pattern.
